extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Kantian philosophy and aesthetics; readers studying the Critique of Judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Kantian criteria for forming and evaluating aesthetic (judgements of taste and the sublime) and teleological judgements (purposiveness in nature and organisms). Geared to close study of Kant's Critique of Judgement and its editorial introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: The judgement of taste is aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is aesthetical (i.e. concerned with feeling rather than with concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant treats the judgement of taste as belonging to feeling (pleasure/pain) and not to the faculty of concepts; it occupies an intermediate position between Understanding and Reason. Evaluate aesthetic judgements as responses of feeling, not as conceptual/theoretical assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of satisfaction in judgement of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction which determines the judgement of taste is disinterested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pure judgement of taste requires pleasure that is independent of personal interest (neither desire to possess the object nor moral/other practical interests). Anti-pattern: judging beauty because one wants to own or benefit from the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in the pleasant is bound up with interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in the pleasant is bound up with interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasures called 'pleasant' are tied to inclinations and desires; they are not the form of pleasure proper to judgements of taste. Distinguish mere sensory pleasure (interest-driven) from disinterested aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction in the good is bound up with interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in the good is bound up with interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral or practical good produces satisfaction connected to ends or purposes; this is different from the disinterested satisfaction of taste. Avoid conflating moral approval with aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Beautiful: universal satisfaction apart from concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beautiful is that which apart from concepts is represented as the object of a universal satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgement of beauty claims a universal validity (we expect others to agree) even though it is not grounded in a determinate concept. Scoring note: judge whether an aesthetic judgement purports to be universally communicable despite lacking conceptual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of satisfaction in judgement of taste is subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality of the satisfaction is represented in a judgement of Taste only as subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant holds the universal claim of taste is subjective necessity (we feel entitled to expect agreement), not an objective rule. Evaluate whether a claimed universality stems from feeling (sensus communis) rather than objective properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without definite purpose (formal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste has nothing at its basis but the form of the purposiveness of an object (or of its mode of representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beautiful objects are judged purposive in form though not purposive for an external end. Criterion: does the object's form appear 'as if' adapted to cognitive faculties without representing a specific function?

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgements rest on a priori grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste rests on a priori grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that pure aesthetic judgements are grounded in a priori conditions of our judging faculty. When evaluating claims of pure taste, assess whether they appeal to a priori principles rather than empirical contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure judgement of taste independent of charm and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The pure judgement of taste is independent of charm and emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure judgements exclude incidental charms (sensory allurements) and transient emotions. Anti-pattern: counting mere charm, colorful stimulus, or strong emotion as constitutive proof of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of free and dependent beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction between free beauty (independent of a concept of what the object should be) and dependent beauty (beauty under a definite concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free beauty: judged solely by form; dependent beauty: judged in relation to a concept (e.g., beauty of a portrait as conforming to a standard). Pure taste concerns free beauty; dependent beauty is not 'pure'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste independent of concept of perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is quite independent of the concept of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is not to be equated with perfection or completeness of properties; assess whether aesthetic praise is rooted in perceived purposiveness/form rather than notions of perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: The subjective necessity of aesthetic judgements (sensus communis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjective necessity which we ascribe to the judgement of taste is conditioned by the Idea of a common sense (sensus communis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Our claim that others ought to agree in taste presupposes a sensus communis—a shared standard of judging. Evaluate whether the aesthetic claim presumes communicability and common cognitive faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have we ground for presupposing a common sense?
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether we have ground for presupposing a common sense; the necessity of universal agreement in taste is a subjective necessity represented as objective under this presupposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing assertions of universal taste, examine whether the author justifies presupposing a shared cognitive ground rather than asserting objective features in the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability of sensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction and analysis include the communicability of a sensation as part of judgements of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgement involves the expectation that the felt pleasure is communicable; good aesthetic argument attends to the way feelings can be shared or expressed to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as a kind of sensus communis
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is a kind of sensus communis (a common sense) enabling communicable judgements of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgements of taste are evaluated by their claim to be communicable via shared faculties; consider whether a proposed standard of taste appeals to shared cognitive structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and intellectual interests in the Beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an empirical interest in the Beautiful and an intellectual interest in the Beautiful (distinct bases for appreciation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate pleasures based on empirical inclinations versus those based on intellectual/formal response. Critiques should note which interest is operative in a given aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Art in general and Beautiful Art as art insofar as it seems like nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful art is an art in so far as it seems like nature; fine art is the art of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant: great art appears natural (gives rule to art) and stems from genius. Evaluate artworks for the appearance of naturalness (not forced contrivance) and the presence of genius (original aesthetic ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius: innate faculty presenting aesthetical Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is an innate mental disposition through which Nature gives the rule to Art; Genius is the faculty of presenting aesthetical Ideas, to which no concept is adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius is not teachable; its products contain more than can be conceptually expressed. In judging artistic merit, consider originality, the presence of aesthetic ideas, and whether the work transcends explicit rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste must check genius; prefer losing genius to violating taste
rubrics_metrics.description: If in a work of art some feature must be sacrificed, it is better to lose something of genius than to violate the canons of taste; the sanity of true genius expresses itself in self-mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating art, balance originality with adherence to taste/canons; excessive departure that violates taste counts against value despite genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Beautiful vs the Sublime: different relations of subject and object
rubrics_metrics.description: True beauty is found in form (restful contemplation); the sublime excites a mental movement and often arises from formlessness or violation of purpose. The feeling of the sublime expresses a purposiveness of the subject with respect to the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an aesthetic reaction is restful/form-based (beauty) or a dynamic movement involving awe/horror yet not actual fear (sublime). Recognize that sublime judgments concern subject's faculties more than object's form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of the Sublime: Mathematically vs Dynamically Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime divides into the Mathematically Sublime (magnitude) and the Dynamically Sublime (power, nature as might).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical sublime: awe at absolute magnitude beyond comprehension; Dynamical sublime: awe at overwhelming power. In critique, identify which kind of sublimity is claimed and whether the pleasurable 'horror' is disinterested (not real fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sublime awakens idea of supersensible destination (moral feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling of the Sublime awakens in us a feeling of the supersensible destination of man; the principle underlying consent in judging of the sublime is the presupposition of the moral feeling in man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublime judgements often relate to moral ideas and the sense of our supersensible capacities; evaluate claims of sublimity for their moral or regulative implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: No objective principle of taste possible; principle of Taste is subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no objective principle of taste possible; the principle of Taste is the subjective principle of Judgement in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant denies objective rules for taste; when constructing evaluative frameworks, account for the subjectivity and regulative role of taste rather than pretending to objective standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction of aesthetical judgements: method and peculiarities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deduction of aesthetical judgements must account for their peculiarities (communicability, subjective universality) and show what is properly asserted a priori in a judgement of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of aesthetic claims should explicate what aspects are asserted a priori (form of purposiveness, communicability) and what depends on empirical conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective purposiveness of nature: formal vs material purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the objective purposiveness of Nature: distinguish objective purposiveness which is merely formal as distinguished from that which is material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating teleological claims, separate attributions of purposiveness that concern form/adaptation to our cognitive faculties (formal) from attributions claiming actual functional ends (material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative vs inner purposiveness of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the relative, as distinguished from the inner, purposiveness of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative purposiveness: apparent adaptation in relations; inner purposiveness: genuine organised purpose within an organism. Assess whether purpose is ascribed externally (relational) or internally (organismic teleology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Things regarded as natural purposes are organised beings
rubrics_metrics.description: Things regarded as natural purposes are organised beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleological judgement applies appropriately to organisms whose parts exist for the sake of the whole; evaluate claims of purposiveness by checking for reciprocal functional interdependence characteristic of organized beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of judging internal purposiveness in organised beings
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a principle of judging of internal purposiveness in organised beings (their parts exist by means of the others and for the sake of the whole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing purposiveness internally, require evidence of systemic interdependence and circularity of functions rather than simple mechanical causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Teleology as internal principle of natural science (regulative use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of an objective purposiveness of nature is a critical principle of Reason for the reflective Judgement; Teleology functions as a regulative, not a constitutive principle for natural science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat teleological explanations as heuristically valuable for guiding investigation (reflective/regulative), but not as providing constitutive metaphysical proof of ends; avoid dogmatic teleological claims presented as scientific certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antinomy of the Judgement regarding teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation of an antinomy of the Judgement arises in teleological reasoning and must be addressed (dialectic of Teleological Judgement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and resolve antinomies (apparent contradictions) when teleological claims conflict with mechanistic explanations; good critique identifies the limits and proper use of teleological concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary subordination of mechanism to teleological principle in explanation of natural purpose (methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the necessary subordination of the mechanical to the teleological principle in the explanation of a thing as a natural purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that to explain a natural purpose we must subordinate mechanical explanations to teleological considerations methodologically; evaluate explanatory strategies for whether they properly integrate mechanism and teleology without illicitly elevating one to absolute status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism may explain some purposive appearances (e.g., crystallization) but does not eliminate teleology entirely
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples like crystallisation show mechanism can produce beautiful forms; mechanism may explain the semblance of purpose in some cases but not necessarily all organised purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims that Darwinian/mechanistic accounts eliminate teleology, examine whether the explanation truly accounts for internal purposiveness of organisms or only for apparent order; avoid conflating appearance-of-purpose with organismic purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theism as the most satisfactory explanatory ground for purposiveness but only regulatively valid
rubrics_metrics.description: Theism represents natural purposes as produced by the Will and Design of an Intelligent Author and Governor of Nature; it is 'superior to all other grounds of explanation' yet valid only for the reflective, not the determinant Judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant: invoking a designing Cause is a satisfactory human explanation but lacks speculative (objective) justification; in evaluating teleological-theological arguments, distinguish their regulative practical utility from claims of theoretical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral argument: use of practical Reason to justify belief in God (as a moral postulate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral argument does not supply objective proof of God but shows that if one wishes to think in a way consonant with morality, one must admit certain assumptions (God, immortality) under practical Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teleological or aesthetic claims appeal to the moral, assess whether they are being used as practical/regulative postulates rather than theoretical proofs; note Kant's distinction between practical necessity and theoretical certainty.
